meta.title: Computable
meta.description: Learn the Turing machine by running one.

home.title: Computable
home.lead: Computable is a place to learn the Turing machine by running one, step by step.
home.caption: This is Turing's first machine, from his 1936 paper. It prints 0 1 0 1 … on every other cell and never stops.

secret.title: Type a secret message
secret.lead: Enigma turns each letter into another one. Type below, and the lamps light your secret letters.
secret.label: Your message
secret.rules: Enigma has only 26 letters. It drops accents, types X for a space, and leaves out digits and signs.
secret.stays: Your secret stays in this browser. It is never sent anywhere.
secret.hidden: Each new secret gets its own random Enigma key. Home keeps the key hidden.
secret.loadLab: Load my secret into the lab
secret.bombeHint: To break it, the Bombe needs a crib: about 15 letters you know are in your secret.

oneRotor.note: The states p0 to p3 are the 4 positions of the rotor. In each one, the machine writes the letter the rotor gives, moves right, and turns the rotor one step. 4 positions × 4 letters = 16 rules, and 4 more rules stop the machine at the end of the input. The same idea with 26 letters needs 26 × 26 = 676 rules, plus 26 to stop. The <lab>Enigma lab</lab> has 3 rotors and 26 letters.

about.title: About Computable
about.lead: Computable began in 2016 as a capstone project for a degree in Computer Science at UNASP: a Turing machine simulator for the web.
about.rebuilt: In 2026 the author rebuilt it from scratch as Computable. The simulator still opens the machines saved by the 2016 app.
about.project: Simulador de Máquina de Turing, Uma Aplicação Web para o Ensino
about.projectEnglish: (A Turing machine simulator: a web app for teaching)
about.author: Wellmmer Lucas de Oliveira Pinto
about.tag: See the 2016 app's code at the git tag v1.0-tcc-2016

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.lead: Computable has no accounts and keeps no personal data about you. It sets one cookie, only to remember your language.
privacy.browser: Your browser keeps your current machine, your choice of squared or night paper, your language, and whether you saw the tour. They stay on your device.
privacy.quiz: Your quiz results stay in this browser only.
privacy.secret: Home’s secret message, its secret letters and the Enigma settings stay in this browser only. “Forget my secret” deletes them.
privacy.language: The language is also in a cookie named NEXT_LOCALE, for one year. The site sets it when you choose a language, or when you open a page in a language other than your browser's. Your browser sends it with each page request, so the site's main address opens your language. It holds only the language code, such as pt-BR.
privacy.shareLink: A share link holds the machine after the # sign. Browsers do not send that part of a link to any server.

analytics.title: What the site counts
analytics.summary: To learn which pages help people, the site counts visits with {service}. It sets no cookies.
analytics.counted: For each page view it records the time, the page, the page you came from, your country, region and city, your browser, your system and the kind of device.
analytics.address: It counts the page address without the part after the # sign. So it never receives the machine from a share link.
analytics.visitor: It tells visits apart with a code made from the request, and throws the code away after 24 hours. It does not tie the visits to you or to your IP address.

privacy.donations: The Support page only links to payment services, such as PayPal and Ko-fi. You pay on their pages, under their privacy rules. No payment data passes through Computable.

tape.title: The tape
tape.text: The tape is a row of cells. Each cell holds one symbol. The number under a cell is its place.
tape.task: Find cell 0: the input starts there.

head.title: The head and its state
head.text: The red circle is the head. It reads the cell inside it. The tag above it shows the machine's state.
head.task: Press Step and watch the head move one cell.

sentence.title: The step sentence
sentence.text: This sentence says in words what the last step did.
sentence.task: Press Step and read the new sentence.

controls.title: The controls
controls.text: Step does one step, and Step back undoes it. Run plays the machine until it stops. Reset starts again. Each button shows its key.
controls.task: Press Run and watch the machine work.

rules.title: The rule table
rules.text: Each row is one rule: in this state, reading this symbol, write, move, then go to the next state.
rules.task: Press Step and watch which row lights up.

diagram.title: The state diagram
diagram.text: The same rules as circles and arrows. Each circle is a state. The arrow of the last rule turns red.
diagram.task: Press Step and watch the red arrow.

keys.title: Keyboard and examples
keys.text: Pick another machine from the Example list. Press ? at any time to see every keyboard shortcut.
keys.task: Pick an example, then press Finish.

quiz.title: Check what you learned
quiz.intro: Choose one answer for each question, then press Check.
quiz.saved: Your result is saved in this browser only.

encoding.caption: Turing’s first machine, written as a description
encoding.hint: Point at a row, tap it, or move to it with Tab. Its part of the description and of the number is marked.

page.title: Learn
page.lead: Short lessons about the Turing machine. Most lessons have machines you can run. Each lesson ends with a quiz.
page.guideSummary: The paper behind these lessons, part by part: pages, short summaries and quotes, with a tape that runs as you read. No quiz.

reset.question: Clear all your quiz results in this browser?

lesson.license: The text of this lesson is under the <link>CC BY 4.0</link> license. You may share and adapt it if you credit Computable.

paper.title: Turing’s 1936 paper
paper.lead: A reading guide to Turing’s paper “On Computable Numbers”, one part at a time. Each part has its pages in the journal and a short summary. Most parts also have a quote and links to the lessons that explain them.
paper.source: The paper: A. M. Turing, “On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem”, Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society, series 2, volume 42, pages 230–265. <link>doi.org/10.1112/plms/s2-42.1.230</link>
paper.notice: This guide quotes the paper and does not reproduce it.
paper.tapeIntro: The tape at the top runs Turing’s first machine, from section 3. Each part you reach moves it one step. If your device asks for less motion, use the Step and Reset buttons instead.
paper.tapeNoScript: The tape needs JavaScript to move.
paper.readCorrection: Read the correction on the publisher’s site
paper.license: The text of this guide is under the <link>CC BY 4.0</link> license. The quotes from Turing’s paper are not.

page.lead: Type a letter on your keyboard or tap a key. A lamp lights the secret letter.

messages.title: Messages to decrypt
messages.lead: Load a message into the machine, then type its secret letters. The lamps light the message.
messages.spaces: Enigma has no space key, so operators typed X between words.
messages.keyGroup: The first group, {group}, only named the key. It is left out here.
messages.hiddenStart: The operator sent the start hidden: from {from}, typing {typed} lights {start}.

barbarossa.title: Operation Barbarossa, 1941
barbarossa.about: On 7 July 1941, a German division in Russia sent this report in 2 parts. Frode Weierud and Geoff Sullivan broke it, in their project to break German wartime messages.
barbarossa.rules: X is a space, Q often stands for CH, and names are written twice.
barbarossa.text: Reconnaissance unit from Kurtinowa, north-west of Sebez, on the flight corridor towards Dubrowki and Opotschka. Set off at 18:30. Attack: Infantry Regiment 3 moves forward slowly but surely. 17:06: 1st Battalion, Infantry Regiment 3, on the flight corridor, its front 16 km east of Kamenec. Division commander.

scharnhorst.title: The Scharnhorst’s last message, 1943
scharnhorst.about: On 26 December 1943, the German warship Scharnhorst sent this message in its last battle. It sank soon after. The M4 Project broke the message on 28 May 2008.
scharnhorst.rules: J comes before and after the place name. AAA CCC stands for the square AC.
scharnhorst.text: Am steering for Tanafjord. Position: square AC 4992. Speed: 20 knots. Scharnhorst.

decrypt.title: Decrypting: {title}
decrypt.help: Type these letters, or press “Type it for me”. The lamps light the message.
decrypt.soFar: So far, so good: {right} of {total} letters are right. Keep typing.
decrypt.wrong: Letter {at} is not right. Backspace takes letters back.
decrypt.partial: The Bombe found only some plug pairs. Letters it did not reach may come out wrong.

page.title: Bombe
page.lead: Give the Bombe a word you know is in the message. It finds the key.

crib.title: Crib
crib.secretHelp: Paste the secret letters of a message. Spaces do not matter.
crib.practiceAbout: The practice message is a made-up German weather report. It starts with WETTERBERICHT, “weather report”.
crib.barbarossaAbout: Part 1 of the Barbarossa message, a real German army report from 7 July 1941. The crib {crib} comes from its known text: “Kurtinowa nordwestl. Sebez”.
crib.barbarossaRings: The real key used rings {rings} and start {start}. The Bombe assumes rings A A A, so it finds start {found} instead. With rings A A A, the middle rotor turns at other letters. So the stop’s key reads the message in blocks of about 15 letters, with wrong letters between them.
crib.crib: Crib: a word you know is in the message
crib.lined: Secret letters at this place: {secret}. Crib: {crib}.
crib.fits: No letter turns into itself here.
crib.crashes: {count, plural, one {# letter would turn into itself (red).} other {# letters would turn into themselves (red).}} Enigma never does that, so the crib cannot sit here.
crib.tooLong: The crib is longer than the secret letters.
crib.hintShort: Tip: use a crib of {count} letters or more. A short crib gives many false stops.
crib.hintNoLoop: Tip: this menu has no loop. Slide the crib or make it longer to get fewer false stops.

menu.legend: Each line is one crib letter on its secret letter. The test starts at {center}, the letter with the most lines.

slow.title: One test, step by step
slow.about: Watch how the Bombe tests one rotor order and one start. It takes the first stop of the last search, or the practice message’s key, or the rotor order and start on the drum wall.
slow.enter: The test current enters {letter} on wire {wire}. This is the guess “{letter} is plugged to {wire}”.
slow.link: Through link {number} ({plain} on {cipher}), {from} on wire {fromWire} lights {to} on wire {toWire}.
slow.mirror: The diagonal board adds the mirror wire: {letter} on wire {wire}.
slow.noStop: All 26 wires of {center} lit: no stop.
slow.stop: Stop: only {lit} of 26 wires of {center} lit.
slow.clash: Only {lit} of 26 wires of {center} lit. But every guess for {center} gives a letter two partners, so this is not a stop.

history.title: How the Bombe came to be
history.lead: Each fact links to the pages we checked it against.

bomba.title: 1938: the Polish bomba
bomba.text: Marian Rejewski of the Polish Cipher Bureau designed the bomba in 1938. It searched for the daily Enigma settings by machine. The Poles ran 6 bomby side by side, one for each rotor order.

pyry.title: July 1939: the meeting at Pyry
pyry.text: On 25 and 26 July 1939, Polish, French and British codebreakers met at Pyry, near Warsaw. The Poles shared what they knew about Enigma. In August, they sent one copy of the Enigma to Paris and one to London.

turing.title: 1939: Turing’s Bombe
turing.text: Alan Turing designed the British Bombe in 1939. It worked from a crib, a word known to be in the message. Its name comes from the Polish bomba, but it worked in another way. The British Tabulating Machine Company built it in Letchworth, under the engineer Harold “Doc” Keen.

victory.title: March 1940: Victory
victory.text: The first Bombe, called Victory, started work at Bletchley Park in March 1940. One source says it started on 14 March. Another says it arrived on 18 March.

welchman.title: August 1940: Welchman’s diagonal board
welchman.text: Gordon Welchman invented the diagonal board. It uses one fact: if A is plugged to B, then B is plugged to A. The board removed many false stops. The first Bombe with the board, Agnus, was installed on 8 August 1940.

film.title: On film
film.text: The Imitation Game (2014), a drama with Benedict Cumberbatch as Alan Turing.
film.changes: The drama changes facts: Turing did not design the Bombe alone, and Gordon Welchman does not appear in the film. The film calls the machine “Christopher”, but the first real Bombe was called Victory.
